title: Whering vs Indyx vs Stylebook (2026): Which to Choose
h1: Whering vs Indyx vs Stylebook: which wardrobe app suits you in 2026
excerpt: Whering vs Indyx vs Stylebook compared on price, platforms, outfit tools, wear stats and privacy, with a quick verdict for every kind of user.
tldr: Pick Stylebook if you use an iPhone or iPad and want a one-time purchase with detailed wear stats and no account. Pick Whering if you want a free app on iPhone, Android and the web that shuffles outfits for you and has a social side. Pick Indyx if you want a free, unlimited closet with cost per wear on iPhone or Android, and the option of a human stylist.
body:
Whering vs Indyx vs Stylebook mostly comes down to two things: which phone you use, and how much help you want putting outfits together. Stylebook is a one-time purchase for iPhone and iPad, with detailed wear statistics and no account. Whering is free on iPhone, Android and the web, shuffles outfits for you and has the biggest social side. Indyx is free on iPhone, iPad and Android with unlimited items, and offers paid human stylists instead of AI outfit suggestions.

This comparison uses each app's official website and its US App Store and Google Play listings, checked on 17 October 2026. We haven't tested the apps ourselves. Prices and features change often, so check the listing before you pay for anything.

Quick verdict by type of user

  • You use Android: Whering or Indyx. Stylebook has no Android version, and its FAQ says there are no plans for one "at the moment". Our guide to Stylebook alternatives for Android covers more options.
  • You want to pay once and skip the account: Stylebook, on iPhone or iPad.
  • You want wear tracking and cost per wear without paying: Indyx. The free tier includes unlimited items, outfits and calendar entries, and cost per wear is calculated automatically.
  • You want the app to come up with outfits: Whering, with its Dress Me shuffler and, on iPhone since October 2026, planner suggestions based on your wardrobe and the weather.
  • You'd rather pay a person than trust an algorithm: Indyx, which sells sessions with human stylists.
  • You want to use a laptop as well as your phone: Whering, which has a web version. Neither Indyx nor Stylebook lists one.

Sources: Whering's App Store and Google Play listings, Indyx's App Store and Google Play listings, and Stylebook's App Store listing and features page.

Whering vs Stylebook

Of the three pairs, this is the clearest split. Whering is a free, online, social app that runs on almost any phone. Stylebook is a paid-once, private tool that runs only on Apple's phones and tablets.

Cost. Stylebook costs $4.99 once in the US, according to its FAQ, and the App Store lists no in-app purchases. Whering's site says you can use it for free to manage and style your closet. Its paid extras are a Style Pass, which opens up the Outfit Maker, plus credit packs and optional supporter tiers. The listing doesn't spell out every free limit, so check inside the app.

Getting clothes in. Both remove photo backgrounds. Whering also lets you add pieces from a database of more than 100 million items or straight from retailer sites, which helps if you'd rather not photograph your whole wardrobe. Stylebook has a store clipper, and its Instant Import uses AI to cut items out of photos.

Making outfits. Stylebook suits people who like to arrange outfits themselves on a free-form canvas, with Outfit Shuffle for when you want a random mix. Whering leans the other way. Dress Me shuffles your pieces into outfits, and an October 2026 iPhone update made the planner suggest outfits based on your wardrobe and the weather.

Stats. Both track cost per wear. Stylebook adds closet value and top 10 lists of your most and least worn pieces. Whering adds wear rate, intake tracking, your colour palette and closet longevity. If the goal is spotting the grey hoodie you wear weekly and the linen blazer you've worn twice, either will do it, provided you log what you wear.

Privacy and updates. Stylebook keeps your closet on your device and in iCloud if you turn sync on, and its App Store label lists only usage data, not linked to you. Whering is an online account, and its App Store label lists identifiers used to track you. One point against Stylebook: its last App Store update was version 10.1 in June 2025, and it needs iOS or iPadOS 17 or later. Whering was updated in October 2026.

Choose Whering if you use Android or switch between devices, want outfit ideas without arranging them yourself, or like browsing friends' closets. Choose Stylebook if you're staying on iPhone or iPad, prefer to build every outfit by hand and want your closet stored on your device rather than in an app company's account.

Indyx vs Stylebook

These two have more in common than either has with Whering. Both are for people who like to organise and plan by hand, and neither generates outfits for you. Indyx is blunt about it: its App Store listing promises "No random outfits styled by robots".

The big differences are price, platform and data. Indyx's core app is free with unlimited items, outfits, calendar entries and packing lists, and it runs on Android as well as iPhone and iPad. The optional Indyx Insider membership, listed on the US App Store at $12.99 a month or $74.99 a year in October 2026, adds extra analytics and outfit-of-the-day selfies. Stylebook asks for $4.99 once and nothing after that, but it only works on iPhone and iPad.

For cataloguing, Indyx has shortcuts Stylebook lacks. You can add a piece by forwarding a shopping receipt or pasting a product link, and AI tags each item's category, subcategory and colour. Stylebook gives you more fields to fill in yourself (notes, tags, season, colour, brand, fabric, size and a link) and more outfit tools, including Clone Outfit, mini mood boards and an inspiration library. On devices with Apple Intelligence it can also generate clothing images from a text description.

Both calculate cost per wear. Indyx does it automatically and lets you sort your closet by wears. Stylebook adds closet value and its Style Stats lists.

The other difference is people. Indyx's site lists a virtual stylist starting at $60, a 10-outfit Lookbook starting at $150 and a three-outfit Lookbook Mini starting at $60. In select US metro areas, an "Archivist" will come to your home and catalogue your wardrobe for you.

Go with Indyx if you're on Android, want a free closet with no item cap, or might pay a stylist later. Go with Stylebook if you're on iPhone or iPad and prefer a single payment, no account and the more detailed outfit canvas.

Whering vs Indyx

If you use Android, or your household has both kinds of phone, these are the two to choose between. Both are free to start, both run on iPhone and Android, and both remove backgrounds, track cost per wear, plan outfits ahead and make packing lists. The real difference is who does the styling.

Whering leans on the app. Dress Me shuffles your clothes into outfits, the Outfit Maker builds them once you have a Style Pass, and the iPhone planner now suggests outfits from your wardrobe and the weather. Indyx leans on people. You build outfits yourself on drag-and-drop boards, and if you want help, you book a human stylist.

They charge differently too. Whering sells one-off in-app purchases such as the Style Pass and credit packs. Indyx sells a subscription, Insider, plus stylist sessions. Both work as free apps if you never pay, but Whering's Outfit Maker and Indyx's extra analytics sit behind those payments.

Scale and social life differ. Whering's Google Play listing shows 5 million-plus downloads to Indyx's 100,000-plus, and it has more social features: friends' closets, style submissions, moodboards and wishlists. Indyx's sharing is quieter, limited to sharing your closet with friends and browsing other people's Open Closets. Whering also works in a web browser and through a Chrome extension; Indyx doesn't list a web app.

On data, Indyx's Google Play listing says no data is shared with third parties, and its App Store label has no "used to track you" section, though it does list contact details, identifiers and payment info linked to you, including for advertising or marketing. Whering's Google Play listing says photos and videos may be shared with third parties, and its App Store label lists identifiers used to track you. Both offer deletion on request.

Pick Whering if you want the app to suggest outfits, use a laptop as well as your phone, or enjoy the social side. Pick Indyx if you'd rather style yourself, want fewer data-sharing flags on the store listings, or like having a human stylist as an option.

Privacy and account notes

The three apps handle your closet in quite different ways. The labels below are declared by the developers themselves on the App Store and Google Play, so treat them as a starting point rather than an audit.

  • Stylebook: stored on your device, and in iCloud if you enable it. No account system is described. App Store label: usage data only, not linked to you. Backups go through iCloud, which needs free iCloud storage.
  • Whering: an online account with web sign-in. App Store label: name, email, phone number, product interaction and crash data linked to you, plus identifiers used to track you. Google Play: may share photos and videos with third parties; data encrypted in transit; deletion on request.
  • Indyx: an online closet. App Store label: contact info, user ID, device ID, payment info and product interaction linked to you, including for advertising or marketing. Google Play: no data shared with third parties; deletion on request.

Whichever you choose, check the background before you upload a mirror photo. A bedroom, a window view or a letter on a desk can give away more than you meant to. Our guide to the downsides and privacy risks of wardrobe apps lists what else to look at.

Who should pick which

Staying on iPhone and building outfits by hand. Stylebook. It's cheap, private and thorough for manual planning. The risk is the update gap, with no new version since June 2025. If that worries you, Indyx is the closest free alternative on iPhone.

Moving from iPhone to Android. Set up Whering or Indyx before you switch. Stylebook's backups go through iCloud, which helps on a new iPhone or iPad but not on Android, and its FAQ doesn't describe an export to other apps. Whering keeps your closet in an online account you can also open on the web, and Indyx is on both platforms; confirm your closet shows up on the new phone before you wipe the old one.

A mixed household, or a laptop habit. Whering, the only one of the three with a web version.

Wearing a fraction of what you own. Indyx, free. Log what you wear for a month, sort by wears, and the pieces you never reach for show up quickly. Stylebook's least-worn top 10 does the same job on iPhone.

Stuck for ideas every morning. Whering's shuffler and planner suggestions. If you want something more AI-led, look at the alternatives below.

A big event and no time. Indyx's Lookbook or a virtual stylist session. It costs real money, from $60 on its site, but it's the only option here where a person puts the outfits together for you.

Alternatives to Whering, Indyx and Stylebook

If none of the three fits, these are the apps they're most often compared with. Our list of the best digital wardrobe apps covers them in more depth, and the round-up of free AI wardrobe tools covers free AI options.

  • Google Photos Wardrobe: builds a closet automatically from clothes in photos of you, lets you combine up to six items into an outfit and try it on virtually. As of October 2026 it's only in the US, Brazil and India, and Google's help page says it's rolling out to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers "as well as other select users"; non-subscribers need more than 1,000 photos of themselves. It comes with Google Photos if you're eligible.
  • Fits: often compared with Whering. Free with unlimited items and background removal, with a swipe outfit builder and a free canvas, on iPhone and Android. Unlimited AI suggestions and AI tagging come with Fits Pro. No web app.
  • Acloset: AI daily outfit suggestions based on weather and your schedule, plus a calendar and cost per wear. Free for up to 100 items, with ads; subscriptions for more.
  • Alta: AI daily outfits, avatar try-on and packing lists on iPhone, Android and the web. Free, with no in-app purchases listed on the App Store, though it also suggests pieces to buy.
  • GetWardrobe: syncs across Android, iPhone, iPad, Mac and the web. Free for up to 100 items (clothes and outfits combined), with a Premium subscription beyond that.
  • FitWardrobe: FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet. It's coming to Android and the web, and iPhone users will be able to use the web version. You photograph a piece and AI tags its type, colour, pattern, season and formality, which you can correct. Pick an occasion and it builds a complete outfit only from clothes you own, with a one-line reason and one or two alternatives. Your wardrobe is stored on your device; tagging sends a compressed photo to Google's Gemini API and suggestions send item details to Groq, so the AI features need an internet connection (more on our AI transparency page). It has no calendar, wear tracking, packing lists or social features, so it doesn't replace any of the three above. It will be free during early access, and you can join the early-access list to hear when it opens.

faq.a: Neither is better for everyone. Whering suits people who want the app to suggest outfits, a web version and social features. Indyx suits people who prefer to build outfits themselves, want unlimited free items with automatic cost per wear, or might pay a human stylist. Both are free to start on iPhone and Android, so try each with ten pieces before committing.

faq.q: Are Whering, Indyx and Stylebook free?
faq.a: Whering and Indyx are free to download and use for their core features. Whering sells optional extras such as a Style Pass for its Outfit Maker; Indyx sells an Insider membership and human stylist sessions. Stylebook isn't free: its FAQ lists a one-time charge of $4.99 in the US, with no subscription. Prices vary by country, so check your store listing.

No. Stylebook's FAQ says it is only available for iPhone and iPad, and it answers the Android question with 'Not at the moment. As of 2025, we are focusing on iOS.' It doesn't run on desktop computers either. On Android, Whering and Indyx are the closest of the three to it, and both are free on Google Play.

faq.q: Does Indyx have AI outfit suggestions?
faq.a: No. Indyx uses AI to tag new items by category, subcategory and colour, but it doesn't generate outfits. Its App Store listing promises 'No random outfits styled by robots' and points to paid human stylists instead. If you want automatic suggestions, Whering's Dress Me shuffler and planner, or AI-first apps such as Acloset and Alta, are a closer fit.

faq.q: What are the best apps like Whering?
faq.a: Indyx is the closest free alternative on both iPhone and Android, with unlimited items and cost per wear. Fits offers a free canvas outfit builder and unlimited items. Acloset and Alta suggest outfits with AI, and GetWardrobe syncs across Android, Apple devices and the web. In the US, Brazil and India, eligible users can also try Google Photos Wardrobe.

faq.q: Can I use Whering on a computer?
faq.a: Yes. Whering has a web version you sign in to from a browser, plus a Chrome extension for adding items from shopping sites. Indyx doesn't list a web app, and Stylebook's FAQ says it doesn't run on desktop or laptop computers. If cataloguing on a big screen matters to you, that's a point in Whering's favour.
